issues.legal_issue: Employees of an incorporated government company are not government servants merely because the government owns or controls the company.
material_facts: The employer was an incorporated government company operating an industrial establishment.
The workers were engaged as casual or daily-rated workers in that establishment, rather than appointed as government servants under government service rules.
issues.conclusion: The workers were not government servants and could not claim the status-based protections applicable to government servants on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State of Bihar and A.K. Bindal v. Union of India, an incorporated government company remains distinct from the government, and its employees are not civil servants merely because of government ownership or control. The distinction is consistent with Union Public Service Commission v. Girish Jayanti Lal Veghela: government employment may carry status under Articles 16, 309 and 311 of the Constitution, unlike employment in a government company. Pyare Lal Sharma v. Managing Director is also relied on for the rule that employees of a government company do not receive Article 311 protection.

predicates.employer_is_incorporated_government_comp: The employer is an incorporated company owned or controlled by the government.
predicates.workers_are_company_employees: The workers are employed by the incorporated company, rather than appointed to government service.

issues.definition: When workers are employed by an incorporated government company, they are not government servants.

issues.legal_issue: Long service as a casual or daily-rated worker, including completion of the applicable work threshold, does not by itself create a right to regularization.
material_facts: The workers were engaged as casual or daily-rated horticulture labourers under settlements governing the distribution of available work.
They claimed to have worked beyond the applicable annual work threshold over several years and sought regularization.
The employer stated that horticulture work was intermittent, that there were no gardener posts, and that manpower recruitment was frozen.
The workers identified no statutory rule entitling them to regularization.
issues.conclusion: The workers were not entitled to regularization merely because they had completed the applicable work threshold or had worked for a long period.
issues.legal_principle: Madhyamik Shiksha Parishad v. Anil Kumar Mishra and M.P. Housing Board v. Manoj Shrivastava establish that completion of 240 days does not confer a right to regularization; it imposes certain obligations on termination under the Industrial Disputes Act. Gangadhar Pillai v. Siemens Ltd. and Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Workman, Indian Drugs & Pharmaceuticals Ltd. affirm that daily wagers have no vested right to regularization and that regularization must accord with applicable rules. B.N. Nagarajan v. State of Karnataka, approved in Secretary, State of Karnataka v. Uma Devi, distinguishes curing a procedural irregularity in an appointment from granting permanence; regularization cannot contravene applicable rules. The Industrial Disputes Act provides limited protections concerning lay-off, retrenchment, transfer and closure, including under Sections 25-C, 25-F, 25-FF and 25-FFF.

rule.if: regularization_claim_in_writ_proceeding and casual_or_daily_wage_employment and threshold_service_completed and no_applicable_rule_supports_regularization

predicates.regularization_claim_in_writ_proceeding: Workers ask a court in a writ proceeding to regularize their employment.
predicates.casual_or_daily_wage_employment: The workers are engaged on a casual or daily-wage basis rather than appointed to regular posts.
predicates.threshold_service_completed: The workers have completed the applicable work threshold or otherwise rely on lengthy service.
predicates.no_applicable_rule_supports_regularizati: No applicable rule is identified that entitles the workers to regularization.

issues.definition: When casual or daily-wage workers seek regularization in a writ proceeding based on service alone and no applicable rule supports it, the service does not create a right to regularization.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot direct the absorption or continuation of casual workers, or payment of regular-employee wages, where doing so requires executive employment decisions unsupported by an applicable rule or available posts.
material_facts: A writ court directed the employer to absorb workers for work available on a perennial basis, pay them regular-employee wages, and continue other workers under a settlement pending the availability of perennial work.
The employer stated that horticulture work was intermittent, that no gardener posts existed, and that available work was allocated in approved man-days.
The workers identified no statutory rule supporting continued service or payment of regular wages.
The employer appealed against the writ court's directions, which had been affirmed on appeal.
issues.conclusion: The directions for absorption, regular wages and continued employment could not stand; the lower-court judgments were set aside and the workers' writ petitions were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Workman, Indian Drugs & Pharmaceuticals Ltd. holds that creation and abolition of posts and regularization are executive functions, and that courts cannot direct absorption, continuation in service or payment of regular salaries without an applicable rule. It relies on P.U. Joshi v. Accountant General, Ahmedabad for the executive character of creation and abolition of posts and on Secretary, State of Karnataka v. Uma Devi for the principle that directing a casual or daily-rated worker to continue until superannuation amounts to impermissible regularization. The court must respect the separation of powers and exercise judicial restraint.

predicates.appeal_challenges_writ_employment_direct: An appeal challenges a writ court's directions concerning workers' employment.
predicates.writ_order_directs_absorption_or_continu: The writ court directs that casual workers be absorbed, kept in service, or paid regular-employee wages.
predicates.no_available_post_or_applicable_rule_sup: No available post or applicable rule supports the employment direction.
predicates.work_is_not_continuous: The work for which the casual workers are engaged is intermittent rather than continuous.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges employment directions unsupported by a post or applicable rule for intermittent work, the court must not direct absorption, continuation or regular wages.

issues.legal_issue: Workers may enforce the terms of a settlement in accordance with law if their employer violates it, even though the settlement does not entitle them to the separate relief of regularization.
material_facts: The parties had entered into settlements governing the preference and distribution of available work among land losers and other casual workers.
The workers sought regularization and other employment benefits beyond the terms of those settlements.
The court dismissed the claims for the requested relief but expressly preserved the workers' ability to enforce the settlements if the employer violated them.
issues.conclusion: The workers were not granted regularization, but they remained entitled to enforce any violated settlement terms in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on the terms of the settlements and made clear that any breach could be pursued in accordance with law. The settlements did not furnish a basis for the separate relief of regularization sought in the writ petitions.

predicates.employment_dispute_involves_settlement: The workers' employment arrangements are governed in part by a settlement with the employer.
predicates.employer_violates_settlement_terms: The employer fails to comply with a term of that settlement.

issues.definition: If a settlement governs an employment dispute and the employer violates its terms, the workers may enforce those terms in accordance with law.
